opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say we're still very early, and in some ways we've only just started asking the right questions.

Much of the current alignment work assumes there's a single target to align to: one notion of "helpful," "harmless," or "good." In practice that target is usually set by a fairly narrow group of people, such as the annotators who were hired, the guidelines a company wrote, or the preferences that happen to dominate the data. Human values aren't like that. They vary across cultures, communities, and individuals, and even one person holds values that conflict depending on the situation. So when we collapse all of that into one reward model or one preference ranking, we lose a lot of the texture, and we risk quietly imposing one worldview at enormous scale.

What I find encouraging is that the community is becoming more aware of this. People are now asking questions like: whose values are we encoding? How do we represent disagreement rather than averaging it away? Can a model reason about the fact that different people might reasonably reach different moral judgments about the same situation? That's the direction I think matters most. It's less about finding the one correct answer and more about building models that understand pluralism. A model should be able to say, "Here's how someone with this perspective might see it, and here's how someone else might see it," and also know when a question really does have a broadly shared answer.

There's also a deeper scientific challenge. Values aren't just preferences you can collect with thumbs-up and thumbs-down. They involve commonsense understanding of social norms, of context, and of what people intend and what consequences follow. A lot of my own interest comes from that angle. You can't truly align a system with human values if it doesn't have a robust grasp of how the human world works. Current models are impressive, but their understanding can be surprisingly brittle. They can sound very wise in one phrasing and fail badly in a slightly different one.

So my overall assessment is that there's a lot of energy and some real progress, especially in recognizing the problem. But methodologically we're still leaning heavily on techniques built for a one-size-fits-all world. The next phase, I hope, will involve much more interdisciplinary work, bringing in philosophers, social scientists, and communities who are usually left out of the data. It should also be more transparent about the normative choices we're making, because those choices are being made either way. It's better to make them deliberately and openly.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison between frontier models and less-curated or less-safety-worked open-source models.

r003.rationale: It does not present algorithmic innovation as a way to overcome data limitations; it instead calls for pluralism, interdisciplinary work, and greater transparency.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. So, I think the honest assessment is that we are much earlier than the field sometimes presents itself as being. A lot of what we call alignment today is really alignment to a fairly narrow slice of humanity, and often it's alignment to whatever preferences happened to be captured in the annotation process, which tends to be dominated by particular demographics, particular languages, particular cultural assumptions about what counts as helpful or harmful.

And the deeper issue is that "diverse human values" is not just a dataset problem. Human values are pluralistic, they're sometimes in genuine conflict, and they're contextual. What's appropriate in one community or one situation can be inappropriate in another, and people reasonably disagree. So if the goal is to collapse all of that into a single reward signal and optimize against it, I think that's the wrong framing from the start. You end up with a kind of averaged-out value system that doesn't actually reflect anyone, and that quietly erases minority perspectives in the process.

Some of the work I've been excited about tries to take the pluralism seriously rather than averaging it away. Thinking about models that can represent multiple value systems, that can recognize when a question is genuinely contested versus when there's broad consensus, and that can reason about the context before responding. We've looked at things like social norms and commonsense moral judgments, and what you find very quickly is that the data itself is messy and disagreement is the norm, not the exception. That disagreement is signal, not noise.

I'd also say the field has a measurement problem. It's very hard to evaluate whether a model is aligned with diverse values when our benchmarks are themselves written from a particular vantage point. So I think we need much more investment in evaluation that involves people from many different backgrounds, and in being transparent about whose values a given system is actually reflecting.

So overall, I'd say promising directions, growing awareness that this is a real problem, but still a very large gap between the aspiration and what current methods actually deliver. And I think some humility is warranted. These are questions that humans have been working on for a very long time without resolving, so we shouldn't expect a training procedure to settle them.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve made meaningful progress, but we’re still very far from solving it. One fundamental challenge is that human values are not a single, consistent set of rules. People disagree, and even the same person can make different judgments depending on the context. That’s not necessarily a flaw—it’s part of what makes this problem difficult.

So when we say that a model is aligned with human preferences, we need to ask: whose preferences? Who provided the feedback, what situations were they considering, and whose perspectives were missing? Getting a model to produce answers that a group of annotators prefers is useful, but it doesn’t establish that the model can reason well about competing values in a new situation.

I think we need both better understanding of that diversity and models that can recognize ambiguity. Sometimes the appropriate behavior is to ask a question, acknowledge disagreement, or explain a tradeoff rather than confidently present one answer as universally right. And respecting diverse values still requires thinking carefully about boundaries around harm. That combination is very much an open research problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ve made meaningful progress, but we’re still at a very early stage. We can train models to produce responses that people prefer, but that doesn’t necessarily mean those models understand human values or can reason about them reliably in a new situation.

One fundamental challenge is that human values are not a single, consistent target. People disagree across cultures, communities, and even within the same household. And an individual might prioritize different values depending on the context. So we need to ask: Whose values are we aligning with, and who gets to make that decision?

I think we need to move beyond treating alignment as simply learning the most popular answer. A model should be able to recognize competing considerations, explain why reasonable people might disagree, and ask for context when it matters. Sometimes the appropriate behavior is to acknowledge uncertainty rather than give one confident moral judgment.

And this is not something that technical researchers can solve alone. We need broader participation in deciding what good behavior looks like, alongside better ways to test whether models actually behave that way across different situations.
